answer.shortAnswer: Their content — `string` overloads `==` to perform an ordinal value comparison.
answer.detailedExplanation: For most reference types `==` compares references, but `System.String` overloads `==` and `!=` to compare values (ordinal, case-sensitive). If one operand is typed as `object`, the overload is not used and the comparison becomes a reference comparison — a classic bug. Use `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` for case-insensitive checks.
